items.title: Recent advances in AI are creating a 'paradigm shift' for robotics - Berkeley News
items.summary:
The researchers then gave the AI that simulation and their Graph-as-Policy framework. The AI generated a robot-control program and repeatedly tested and improved it in simulation. When the researchers ran the resulting code on a real robot, it worked.

Six illustrations showing a robotic claw doing various industrial tasks, including hanging items on a wall and pulling cables through different configurations. [...] “AI-powered industrial robots must continuously improve reliability and performance,” said Jeff Mahler, Ambi Robotics’ co-founder and chief technology officer. “Agentic robotics converted production data into robot behavior updates, increasing throughput across our U.S. fleet while keeping engineers in control.” [...] Ken Goldberg, a UC Berkeley roboticist and professor of engineering, said new models make it possible for teams of AI agents to develop robot-control programs, test them in simulated environments and revise the code when something doesn’t work.

items.title: A Way to Invest in AI and Robotics Together
items.summary:
Avid Money & Megatrends readers know that we believe AI and robotics are two of the biggest business and investment trends of the 21st century. They will revolutionize the way we work and play as much as electricity or the automobile did… while creating huge stock market winners along the way.

Tech giant Amazon is uniquely positioned to benefit from both technologies. [...] Amazon operates more than 1,000 warehouses in the U.S. It ships millions of packages across millions of miles every month. This blizzard of activity can become more efficient and profitable with AI-enhanced logistics and robots that don’t complain, don’t take coffee breaks, and don’t ask for raises.

In other words, Amazon is uniquely well-suited to benefit from a megatrend in which robots soon become cheaper, faster, more dexterous, more durable, and smarter. [...] With demand for AI computing power soaring, restrictions on new supply could mean higher prices, greater utilization, and fatter profit margins for AWS.

In other words, Amazon is living up to the label we gave it early this year, when we said the stock was “the best way to invest in AI and robotics at the same time.”

items.title: Using Vibrations and AI, Future Robotic Missions Could Handle Buried Rocks Autonomously - Universe Today
items.summary: As they indicate in their paper, estimating the burial depth of partially embedded rocks is a key capability for energy-limited robotic excavation. When obstacles like rock formations are in the way, mission teams need to know how deep the rock extends so they can decide whether to remove the obstacle or avoid it. Ruan and Komendera's solution leverages AI to interpret vibrational data, allowing robots to make those decisions autonomously. As Komendera said in a Virginia Tech press release: [...] In short, scientists and astronauts need to know what's on a planet's surface (and beneath it) before they attempt to land there and conduct science operations. Thanks to a team from Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University (Virginia Tech), scientists could soon have a new set of tools that will allow robotic missions to make these determinations autonomously. These AI-powered tools measure vibrations in surface terrain to determine what lies beneath and how deep structures extend. [...] These models could help robotic missions excavate subsurface rocks, caches of water ice, and remove obstacles along their travel routes. In the meantime, the team plans to keep building datasets and testing their approach for applications on Earth, such as analyzing construction sites and natural disasters to locate where potentially hazardous materials are buried. They could also be used to study unstable rock formations and underground caverns, assisting with resource and construction
